title: Dataset Distillation via the Wasserstein Metric

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem with a straightforward combination of feature-prototype matching and class-specific BatchNorm regularization, demonstrated at ImageNet-1K scale.

Table I shows consistent improvements over reproduced SRe2L results, including 57.6% versus 54.4% on ImageNet-1K at 50 images per class and 60.7% versus 58.3% at 100 images per class. Strengthening and reporting the reproduced baseline makes these comparisons more credible.

The evaluation includes multiple condensation budgets, three-run accuracy estimates, component ablations, regularization sensitivity, and cross-architecture experiments. The synthetic-image examples suggest improved within-class variety.

The main recovery pipeline and losses are understandable. The manuscript explicitly acknowledges its dependence on SRe2L, established Wasserstein algorithms, DeepInversion-style regularization, and the POT library.
weaknesses: The central contribution is insufficiently distinguished from conventional feature quantization. Section III-D approximates one empirical feature distribution per class with a fixed number of atoms. With freely optimized atom weights and squared Euclidean transport cost, the unregularized objective in Equation (4) is equivalent to k-means quantization. This relationship is neither discussed nor tested. A k-means prototype baseline using the identical recovery pipeline is essential to establish what the Wasserstein formulation contributes.

The optimized probability measure is not clearly connected to the evaluated dataset. Equation (3) and Algorithm 3 introduce learned atom weights, but Algorithm 1 outputs only images, and no corresponding weighted sampling or classifier-training rule is specified. Uniformly training on those images would generally use a different distribution from the one optimized.

The ablations attribute much of the improvement to class-specific BatchNorm rather than the proposed metric. At 10 images per class, the CE-plus-class-specific-BN variant already achieves 64.0/41.3/37.4%, versus 64.8/41.8/38.2% for the full method. These additional gains are useful, but controlled comparisons against MMD and simpler prototype objectives are missing, leaving the claimed superiority of Wasserstein matching insufficiently supported.

Important solver details remain unresolved. Section III-B describes entropy-regularized transport, whereas Appendix A specifies unregularized linear programs. The entropy coefficient, concrete initialization, stopping tolerances, and selected update parameters are not provided. The recovery hyperparameters are documented, but the central barycenter computation is not reproducible unambiguously.

The broader comparative claims exceed the experimental controls. Table I imports several baseline results without establishing matched architectures, resolutions, and soft-label training protocols. Table II provides no competing-method transfer results. Consequently, the strongest evidence supports improvement over the reproduced SRe2L pipeline; broader superiority and comparative generalization remain less established.

The efficiency claim lacks adequate comparative measurement. Table IV measures image-update cost only on 64×64 ImageNette, without accounting separately for feature extraction and barycenter computation or comparing against SRe2L. The reported approximately 14-hour ImageNet experiment demonstrates feasibility, but does not establish the claimed efficiency advantage or its scaling behavior.
